Sup A: bolton_2006_cake_intermediate_blocking · Combined models of membrane fouling: Development and application to microfiltration and ultrafiltration of biological fluids (Cake-intermediate blocking)
The cake-intermediate blocking model describes fouling during filtration of biological fluids through microporous or virus-retention membranes. It predicts permeate volume over time during constant-pressure operation and pressure rise over time during constant-flow operation. The model combines loss of available membrane area through intermediate blocking with increasing flow resistance from cake formation, using Darcy’s law to derive explicit time-dependent equations. The authors evaluated it with human plasma IgG filtered through Durapore PVDF membranes and BSA filtered through Viresolve 180 membranes, under both constant-pressure and constant-flow conditions. They fitted two parameters by minimizing squared residuals and compared its predictions with individual and other combined fouling models.

comparison: The model’s individual blocking and cake-filtration components follow the established blocking-filtration and cake-filtration laws discussed by Grace (1956) and Hermia (1982).

equations: At constant pressure, the model predicts permeate volume as a function of time.

fitting: Model fits were assessed by minimizing the sum of squared residuals between observations and model predictions.

mechanism: In the intermediate-blocking law, available membrane area decreases exponentially with processed permeate volume.
mechanism: Intermediate blocking represents particles sealing some pores while other particles accumulate on previously deposited particles.
mechanism: The cake-filtration law represents increasing resistance as processed volume increases.

results: For constant-flow IgG, the three combined models fit substantially better than the individual fouling models.
results: For constant-pressure BSA, the cake-intermediate and cake-complete fits were within the standard deviation of most data points.
results: For constant-pressure BSA, the cake-intermediate model had an SSR of 9.59 × 10², slightly lower than the cake-complete model’s 1.62 × 10³.

Sup B: ho_2000 · A Combined Pore Blockage and Cake Filtration Model for Protein Fouling during Microfiltration
The model describes protein fouling during microfiltration of bovine serum albumin solutions through polycarbonate membranes. It predicts how filtrate flow and flux decline over time as protein aggregates first cover open membrane areas and a protein deposit then grows over the covered regions. The full model combines flow through uncovered and covered areas and accounts for differences in deposit resistance according to when each region was first covered; the authors also derive a simpler approximate solution. Experiments were run in a stirred cell at constant pressure, with BSA concentration and pressure varied, and the model was compared with measured flux and collected filtrate volume. The authors use it to explain the transition from pore blockage to cake filtration and other observed flux-decline patterns, and to investigate the mechanisms of protein fouling.

system: The model describes bovine serum albumin (BSA) protein fouling during membrane microfiltration.

answer.description: A and B both model protein fouling during membrane filtration by combining a blocking mechanism with cake or deposit growth, and both were evaluated with BSA data. A’s paper describes its combined-model development as extending B; A uses intermediate blocking and cake filtration, while B models pore blockage followed by cake growth over blocked regions. A is a simpler algebraic model with two fitted parameters, whereas B’s full model tracks three evolving quantities and accounts for deposits formed at different times; B also derives an approximate solution. A was tested with BSA and IgG under constant-pressure and constant-flow operation, while B’s experiments used BSA at constant pressure.
